question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer: No. Phasing a creature back in does not trigger "enters the battlefield" abilities. Rule [702.26d] explicitly states that the phasing event doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones or control, even though it's treated as not being on the battlefield while phased out, and that "zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out." Since enters-the-battlefield abilities are zone-change triggers [603.6a], they simply don't fire when a phased-out permanent phases back in. Rule [702.26c] confirms that when a permanent phases in, its status just changes to "phased in" and the game once again treats it as existing — it's a status change, not an actual movement onto the battlefield. This holds true whether phasing happens via the normal untap-step turn-based action [502.1, 703.4a] or via a one-shot effect that phases a permanent out "until" some event [610.4, 610.4a]. Similarly, attach/unattach triggers don't fire when an Aura or Equipment phases in already attached [702.26i, 702.26j]. This answer doesn't depend on the two-player vs. multiplayer distinction, though rule [702.26n] and [800.4a]/[800.4c] note special multiplayer-only cases involving a player leaving the game while a permanent they controlled is phased out.

Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer:
When a creature has both trample and deathtouch, it only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to count as "lethal damage" for trample purposes, and can then assign all remaining damage to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking.

Here's why: rule [702.19b] (Trample) says the controller of an attacking trampling creature must assign lethal damage to each blocking creature before assigning any excess damage to the player/planeswalker/battle it's attacking. Normally "lethal damage" means damage at least equal to the blocker's toughness, minus damage already marked on it (accounting for damage from other sources being assigned in the same step, per [702.19b]).

However, [702.2c] (Deathtouch) specifically overrides this calculation: "Any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt." This is echoed in the general damage-processing rule [120.4a], which says "Any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage if the source dealing that damage to a creature has deathtouch."

So if, say, a 6/6 creature with both trample and deathtouch is blocked by a 4/4 creature, the attacker's controller only needs to assign 1 damage to the 4/4 blocker to satisfy the lethal-damage requirement, and can assign the other 5 damage to the defending player (or planeswalker/battle, if attacking one). The attacker still isn't required to assign lethal damage to the blocker at all, but in that case none of the damage may go through to the player or planeswalker, per [702.19b].

Separately, once even 1 damage from a deathtouch source is actually dealt to a creature with toughness greater than 0, that creature is destroyed as a state-based action per [702.2b] and [704.5h], regardless of how much damage was marked — this destruction is independent of the trample-assignment math and just follows from deathtouch's normal effect once damage is dealt.

Note that trample itself only modifies damage assignment for an attacking creature — it has no effect when a creature is blocking, per [702.19a]. Also, if the creature has trample over planeswalkers instead of (or with) regular trample and is attacking a planeswalker, the deathtouch-reduced lethal amount (1 per blocker) still applies before the attacker needs to assign damage equal to the planeswalker's loyalty, per [702.19c] combined with [702.2c].

This analysis assumes a normal combat damage assignment where no damage has already been marked on the blocking creature(s) before this combat damage step; if damage was already marked (e.g., from a first-strike combat damage step), that marked damage is taken into account when determining how much more is needed to reach the deathtouch-defined 'lethal' threshold, though since deathtouch makes any nonzero amount lethal, in practice as little as 1 damage is enough even after prior damage, per [702.19b].

question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer: Yes. Storm is a triggered ability (rule 702.40a: “Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack. ‘Storm’ means ‘When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn...’”). Because it's a triggered ability and not a spell, it can be affected the same way any other triggered ability on the stack can be: rule 113.9 states that activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, so they can't be countered by effects that counter only spells (like a typical 'counter target spell' effect). However, they CAN be countered by effects that specifically say they counter abilities (e.g., an effect that reads 'counter target ability'). If a card has multiple instances of storm, each one triggers and could in principle be countered separately (702.40b). Note that countering the storm trigger only stops the copying effect — it does not counter the original spell itself, since abilities and spells are separate objects on the stack (603.3, 113.6g).

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer:
No — a card with a hybrid mana symbol counts as ALL of the colors in that symbol for color identity purposes, not just one, so you can't include it unless your commander's color identity contains every one of those colors.

Rule 107.4e states "A hybrid mana symbol is also a colored mana symbol... A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors," and rule 202.2d confirms an object "with one or more hybrid mana symbols... in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols." Color identity (903.4) is defined as the color or colors of any mana symbols in the card's mana cost or rules text. So if a card has, say, a {R/G} hybrid symbol anywhere in its mana cost or rules text, its color identity includes both red and green — even if you only intend to pay the red half (or the green half) when casting it.

Deck construction rule 903.5c requires that every color in a card's color identity also appear in the commander's color identity. So a card with an {R/G} hybrid symbol can only go in a Commander deck whose commander's color identity includes BOTH red and green (e.g., Wort, the Raidmother, whose color identity is red and green per 903.5c's own example). A mono-red or mono-green commander deck cannot include it, because the missing color (green or red, respectively) isn't covered.

This same logic extends to monocolored hybrid symbols like {2/R} — rule 107.4e/202.2d treats those as having the colored component, so {2/R} makes the card red in color identity even though it can be paid entirely with generic mana; it does NOT add an extra color beyond {R} itself in that case, but full two-color hybrid symbols like {R/G} do add both colors.

This is a two-player-independent deck-construction rule, so it applies the same regardless of how many players are at the table.

(Most cards with hybrid mana symbols in their mana costs are printed in a two-tone frame. See rule 107.4e.)

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer:
No. During the untap step, no player receives priority at all, so you cannot cast spells, activate abilities, or otherwise "respond" to anything that happens in that step. This holds true no matter how many players are in the game, since rule 502.4 says "no player receives priority during the untap step" — it isn't framed as a two-player-only rule.

Here's why: the untap step is one of the few steps where turn-based actions occur without any player getting priority [500.3]. In order, phasing happens first [502.1, 703.4a], then (if applicable) the day/night designation check [502.2, 703.4b, 731.2], and finally the active player untaps their permanents [502.3, 703.4c]. None of these use the stack, and rule 502.4 explicitly states that no spells can be cast, no abilities activated, and none of these can resolve during this step because no one has priority. Rule 117.3a confirms the active player normally gets priority at the start of most steps/phases, but calls out the untap step as an exception.

If something triggers during the untap step (for example, a phasing-related or untap-related triggered ability), it doesn't get put on the stack immediately — it's held and put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, which is usually the beginning of the upkeep step, along with any abilities that trigger at the start of upkeep itself [502.4, 503.1a]. Also, rule 500.12 confirms no game events can occur "between" steps, so there's no window between the untap step and upkeep to sneak in a response either.

So practically: you have to wait until the upkeep step, where the active player receives priority [503.1, 503.1a], to cast an instant or activate an ability in response to anything that happened during the untap step.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer: Yes. A creature that has been declared as an attacker remains an attacking creature through the entire combat phase, including the end of combat step, and stops being an attacking creature only when it is removed from combat (for example, by leaving the battlefield, changing controllers, phasing out, etc.) or when the combat phase itself ends — whichever happens first. The end of combat step is the fifth and final step of the combat phase, not a separate phase, so simply reaching that step does not remove creatures from combat. As rule 511.3 states, it's only "as soon as the end of combat step ends" that all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat, and only after that does the combat phase conclude and the postcombat main phase begin. So during the end of combat step itself, attacking creatures are still attacking creatures (and, correspondingly, blocking/blocked/unblocked status also persists until then).

question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer: Yes. Once the evoked creature actually enters the battlefield, it's a normal permanent, and its evoke ability -- "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it" (rule [702.74a]) -- is a triggered ability that goes on the stack and doesn't do anything until it resolves. Between the time it triggers and the time it resolves, the active player and other players get priority in the normal way, and you (or an opponent, if they have an appropriate effect) can sacrifice that creature to some other cost or ability (for example, an unrelated sacrifice outlet) before the evoke trigger ever resolves. Nothing about evoke locks the creature in place while its trigger is pending. If the creature has already left the battlefield by the time the evoke trigger tries to resolve, the instruction 'its controller sacrifices it' simply can't be carried out, since there's no such permanent to sacrifice -- consistent with the general principle that a resolving ability can't force an impossible action [608.2d]. So the evoke trigger doesn't fail to exist or get countered; it just has nothing left to do. Note that this is separate from paying evoke's alternative cost itself: evoke's cost is the mana-substitute cost you announce and pay when casting the spell [702.74a], not a sacrifice -- the sacrifice only happens later, as the effect of the triggered ability once it resolves.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer:
Yes. If an effect causes a permanent to lose all abilities, that includes any keyword abilities it has (flying, trample, deathtouch, etc.), because a keyword ability is just a shorthand name for a full ability that would otherwise be spelled out in the card's rules text — rule [702.1] and [702.1d] confirm that a keyword is simply another way of representing an ability the object has. question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer:
Yes. Your maximum hand size doesn't stop you from drawing cards at any point during the turn — it only matters at cleanup. This is a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack, so it happens automatically at that point in the turn rather than whenever you draw.

Also note maximum hand size itself can be modified (for example, a vanguard card's hand modifier changes both starting hand size and maximum hand size [313.6] [902.5b]), but regardless of what your maximum is, drawing while already at or above it is never illegal — only the end-of-turn discard enforces the limit.

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer:
No. "Dies" is a defined game term that only applies to creatures and planeswalkers — rule 700.4 defines it as "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield," and the keyword-style rule labeled [Dies] specifically states "A creature or planeswalker 'dies' if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield." A non-creature artifact is neither a creature nor a planeswalker, so when it's put into its owner's graveyard from the battlefield, that event is not called it "dying" — it's just going to the graveyard (whether by destruction, sacrifice, or some other effect).

This distinction matters for triggered abilities like "whenever a creature dies" — a plain non-creature artifact going to the graveyard will not trigger that kind of ability, because it never dies (it isn't a creature). However, if an artifact is also a creature (an artifact creature, per rule 300.2, which combines the aspects of both card types), then it is a creature, has power/toughness, and can be destroyed by lethal damage (rules 704.5g, 704.5h) or reduced to 0 toughness (rule 704.5f) and being put into the graveyard from the battlefield in that case does count as dying under rule 700.4. Also note per rule 208.3 that a non-creature permanent (including a plain artifact) has no power or toughness even if printed with some, and per rule 701.8b, "destroyed" only applies to permanents affected by a destroy effect or lethal/deathtouch damage state-based actions — artifacts put into the graveyard some other way (e.g., sacrifice) are not considered destroyed either, just moved to the graveyard.

So: a non-creature artifact never "dies"; only an artifact that is also a creature can die, and only while it's on the battlefield as a creature when it goes to the graveyard.

question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer:
You don't lose the game immediately when you attempt to draw from an empty library — the loss is registered as a state-based action and takes effect the next time any player would receive priority. Specifically, per rule [121.4], a player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game the next time a player would receive priority. Rule [704.5b] confirms this is a state-based action: if a player attempted to draw from an empty library since the last check, that player loses the game. Rule [104.3c] adds the related case where you're required to draw more cards than remain in your library — you draw whatever's left (rule [609.3] similarly says an effect that attempts something impossible does as much as possible) and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority.

A normal draw (rule [121.1]) is putting the top card of your library into your hand, done as a turn-based action in your draw step ([504.1]) or as part of a cost/effect. If your library is empty and you'd draw, the state-based action check (rule [704.1]) will catch it before anyone gets priority again, and you lose at that point — not instantly upon the attempted draw.

One nuance: if an effect merely offers you the choice to draw rather than forcing it, you can still choose to draw even with an empty library (rule [121.3], [121.3a]) — this just means the attempt happens and the same state-based loss applies once you try it. Also, effects that replace a draw (rules [121.6a], [614.11]) still apply even with an empty library, meaning the replacement effect happens instead of an actual empty-library draw attempt, potentially avoiding the loss condition if it replaces the draw entirely.

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer:
In a standard game, the combat phase has five steps, in this order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat [506.1]. (The declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped if no creatures are attacking [506.1].) If any attacker or blocker has first strike or double strike, there are two combat damage steps [506.1].

question: can i respond to a mana ability?
answer:
No. Mana abilities never go on the stack, so there is nothing to respond to — they resolve immediately as soon as they're activated (for activated mana abilities) or immediately after the ability that triggered them (for triggered mana abilities), and they can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to.

Rule 113.4 states that mana abilities "don't use the stack, and, under certain circumstances, a player can activate mana abilities even if they don't have priority." Rule 605.3b spells this out for activated mana abilities: "An activated mana ability doesn't go on the stack, so it can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated." Rule 605.4a says the same for triggered mana abilities: they resolve "immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority."

Because of rule 405.6c, once a mana ability resolves, if the activating player had priority before activating it, they get priority back afterward — but that's just normal priority following the mana ability's resolution, not a response *to* the mana ability. You also don't need priority to activate a mana ability in the first place: per rule 605.3a and 117.1d, a mana ability can be activated whenever a player has priority, or in the middle of casting a spell, activating another ability, or whenever a rule or effect calls for a mana payment. So other players can act right after your mana ability resolves, but they're reacting to the game state (e.g., the fact that you now have mana, or that you're now casting a spell), not responding to the mana ability itself — because by then it has already resolved and no longer exists as an object that could be responded to.

One caveat from rule 605.5a: an ability that looks like it produces mana but has a target, or a triggered ability that could produce mana but is triggered by something other than the activation of a mana ability (or vice versa), is NOT a mana ability under the rules — it's a normal activated or triggered ability that does use the stack and CAN be responded to.

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer:
No. Paying a cost is not itself an event that players get priority to respond to. Paying a cost is simply "carrying out the instructions specified by the spell, ability, or effect that contains that cost" [118.1], and it happens as part of the larger action of casting a spell, activating an ability, or (for attackers/blockers) declaring attackers or blockers — none of which use the stack while the costs are being paid. For example, declaring blockers is a turn-based action that "doesn't use the stack," and the defending player pays all required costs as part of that single action before anyone gets priority [509.1e][509.1f]. The same is true for declaring attackers [508.1j]. Likewise, an activated ability is written as "[Cost]: [Effect]" [602.1], and the cost is paid as part of activating the ability, before the ability is even put on the stack — so there's no window to respond to the payment itself.

The only thing a player can do *during* the process of paying a cost is activate their own mana abilities to generate the mana needed [118.2], since mana abilities don't use the stack and don't cause priority to change [605.1]. That's not "responding" in the sense of an opponent doing something — it's just the same player generating resources to finish paying.

Once the spell has been fully cast or the ability fully activated (all costs paid), it's on the stack, and *that* is when players receive priority and can respond with instants or activated abilities. So you can respond to a spell or ability once it exists on the stack, but not to the act of paying its cost.

question: can you explain layers?
answer:
The layer system (rule 613) is the procedure the game uses to figure out, in a fixed order, how all the continuous effects currently active on an object combine to determine its actual characteristics (power, toughness, color, types, text, abilities, control, etc.) at any given moment. Rule [613.1] says you start with the object's "actual" values (the printed values on a card, or the values set by whatever effect created a token or copy), and then apply all applicable continuous effects in a series of layers, always in the same order:

- Layer 1: Rules and effects that modify copiable values [613.1a] (this layer itself has sublayers, e.g. 1a for copy effects and merging via mutate [613.2, 613.2a]).
- Layer 3: Text-changing effects [613.1c] (see rule 612).
- Layer 4: Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d].
- Layer 5: Color-changing effects [613.1e].
- (The examples under [613.5] and [613.6] also show that there is a Layer 2 for control-changing effects and a Layer 6 for effects that add or remove abilities, and that Layer 7 is split into sublayers such as 7b for power/toughness-setting effects and 7c for power/toughness-modifying effects and counters — the full defining text for those specific layers/sublayers isn't included in the rules given to me, but their existence and relative order is confirmed by the worked examples.)

Within Layer 1 and within Layer 7, there are further sublayers applied in a fixed internal order [613.2, 613.4]. Within any single layer or sublayer, effects are normally applied in timestamp order — the effect that started existing earlier is applied first [613.7]. However, if a dependency exists between two effects in the same layer/sublayer (one effect's existence, applicability, or result changes because of the other), the dependency system overrides the timestamp order [613.8].

An important consequence, per [613.5], is that all of this is continually and automatically recalculated the instant something changes — for example, if a white-anthem effect ("White creatures you control get +1/+1," applied in Layer 7c) is active on a creature and something else changes that creature's color away from white in Layer 5, the anthem stops applying and the creature's power/toughness snaps back immediately, with no separate action needed.

Also, per [613.6], if a single effect has parts that belong in different layers (e.g. "becomes the color of your choice and gets +1/+1"), each part is peeled off and applied in its own layer (color in Layer 5, the +1/+1 in Layer 7c), and once an effect starts applying to a set of objects it keeps applying to that same set in later layers even if the source of the effect is removed in the meantime.

This rule set is written generally (it doesn't reference specific player counts), so the layer system itself works identically whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — nothing in these rules changes based on the number of players.

question: how does the legend rule work?
answer:
If a single player controls two or more legendary permanents that have the same name, a state-based action forces that player to choose one of them to keep, and all the others go to their owners' graveyards. This is called the "legend rule."

Details:
- The legend rule is a state-based action (rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners' graveyards."). State-based actions are checked and applied automatically whenever a player would receive priority, before anyone can respond, so this happens as soon as the duplicate legendary permanents exist under one player's control — no spell or ability triggers it, and no player can act to prevent it once the condition exists.
- It only applies to permanents that have the legendary supertype (rule 205.4d). Legendary instants and sorceries aren't affected by the legend rule itself; instead they have a separate casting restriction — a player can't cast a legendary instant or sorcery unless they control a legendary creature or legendary planeswalker (rule 205.4e).
- "Same name" is what matters, not whether the cards are the literal same card. Two different permanents that happen to share a printed name (for example, two copies of the same legendary card, or a token created with a specific legendary name per rule 111.9) both trigger the rule.
- The comparison is per player: the rule only fires if the *same player* controls both/all of the same-named legendary permanents. If two different players each control a permanent with that name, the legend rule does not apply to either of them, since it's not one player controlling "two or more" of them.
- Planeswalkers that were once restricted by the old "planeswalker uniqueness rule" now instead have the legendary supertype and are subject to the legend rule the same way (rule 306.4).
- Gaining or losing the legendary supertype from other effects doesn't change a permanent's card type, and vice versa (rule 205.4b) — so an effect like "all lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands" wouldn't remove legendary status, and a permanent could still become subject to (or exempt from) the legend rule based purely on whether it currently has the legendary supertype.

Note: the rules given here are the general legend rule; nothing here specifies a distinct multiplayer version, so the mechanic (checked per individual player's own board) works the same regardless of how many players are in the game — it just never compares permanents controlled by different players.

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer:
Your creature isn't destroyed at the exact instant the lethal damage is marked — marking damage and destroying the creature are two separate events. When a source deals damage to a creature, that damage is marked on it immediately [120.3e][302.7]. Dealing that damage does not itself destroy the creature [120.5]. Instead, the game checks state-based actions, and if the total damage marked on the creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, it 'has been dealt lethal damage' and is destroyed as a state-based action [120.6][302.7][704.5g].

State-based actions don't use the stack and aren't something a player does — they happen automatically [704.1][117.2d]. The key timing rule is 117.5: every time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions, repeating until none remain, before that player actually receives priority. So your lethally-damaged creature is destroyed the next time state-based actions are checked, which is generally the moment before any player would next get priority — for example, immediately after the spell or ability that dealt the damage finishes resolving, or, for combat damage, right after damage is dealt simultaneously in the combat damage step (a turn-based action per rule 703.4m) and before priority is passed in that step.

One nuance: the damage itself stays marked on the creature (even if it later stops being a creature) until it's removed — either by regeneration or during the cleanup step [120.6][514.2]. But the destruction check itself happens at the state-based-action checkpoint described above, not merely 'whenever damage happens to be marked.' If you're picturing the damage being marked at some earlier point (e.g., stacked triggers before the SBA check), the creature still won't die until the next SBA check, so it's possible for other triggered abilities checking for damage (rule 120.10, excess damage) to see the marked damage before the destruction occurs.

This explanation applies regardless of player count — none of the rules involved (704, 117.5, 120.6, 302.7) differ between two-player and multiplayer games.

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer:
Generally, no — being your commander does not by itself let you cast the card while it's sitting in exile. Rule 903.8 says "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone," which is the specific permission that lets a commander be cast for the commander tax — it only applies to the command zone, not exile. Rule 601.3f is the general rule: you can only begin to cast a spell if some rule or effect actually allows you to cast it from wherever it currently is; there's no blanket rule letting you cast any card, commander or not, straight out of exile.

What you can do instead: if your commander card is in exile and it got there since the last time state-based actions were checked, rule 903.9a lets you (as its owner) move it into the command zone as a state-based action. Once it's in the command zone, rule 903.8 lets you cast it from there (paying the commander tax for each previous time you've cast it from the command zone this game).

The only way to actually cast it directly from exile is if some other rule or card effect specifically grants permission to cast a card from exile while it's there — for example Plot (rule 702.170d, which lets a plotted card be cast from exile without paying its mana cost) or an Adventure card exiled after resolving as an Adventure (rule 715.3d, which lets you play it later from exile). Absent such an effect, a commander in exile just sits there (or gets moved to the command zone per 903.9a) rather than being castable in place. Note rule 903.3d confirms that 'casting a commander' just means casting a spell that has the commander designation, regardless of what zone it came from — so if a rule does let you cast it from exile, it still counts as casting your commander (and the commander tax in 903.8 would still apply, since that tax is based on how many times you've cast it from the command zone, not on the total number of casts).

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer:
The cleanup step (rule 512.1, 514) is the second and final step of the ending phase, and it normally happens without any player getting priority. Three things happen, in this order:

1. **Discard to hand size.** Immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to get down to that number. This is a turn-based action and doesn't use the stack [514.1] [703.4n].

2. **Damage removed and "until end of turn"/"this turn" effects end.** Immediately after that discard (if any was needed), all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed, and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end. These two things happen simultaneously, and this also doesn't use the stack [514.2] [703.4p]. Any leftover mana in players' mana pools also empties as the step ends, per the general rule that unspent mana empties when a phase or step ends [500.5].

3. **Normally no priority.** Because of this, normally no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated [514.3] [514.3a]. The step simply ends once all these specified actions are completed — it's one of the few steps (along with the untap step) where no one gets priority at all [500.3].

**Exception:** After the actions above, the game checks whether any state-based actions need to be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack (including ones that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"). If either is true, those state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities go on the stack, and the active player then gets priority — players may cast spells and activate abilities as normal. Once the stack is empty and everyone passes in succession, an entirely new cleanup step begins from scratch [514.3a] [704.3]. If nothing like that happens, the step ends with no one getting priority [704.3].

This is the same regardless of how many players are in the game — the cleanup step's rules reference only "the active player" and "any player," so nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer game.

question: when are state-based actions checked?
answer:
State-based actions are checked continuously, but the game only actually performs a check at specific moments: every time a player would receive priority. Per rule [704.3], whenever a player would get priority, the game checks for the listed state-based-action conditions and performs any that apply as a single simultaneous event; if any were performed, the check repeats, and this cycle continues (state-based actions, then any waiting triggered abilities going on the stack, then another check) until nothing more happens, at which point the appropriate player finally gets priority. Rule [117.5] describes the same process from the priority side: before a player gets priority, all applicable state-based actions are performed as a single event, repeated until none occur, then triggered abilities are put on the stack, and this whole loop repeats until it stabilizes and priority is actually given.

State-based actions are not turn-based actions and don't happen automatically 'at the start of a step' the way turn-based actions do ([703.1], [703.3]) — turn-based actions (like the draw step's draw, or the cleanup step's hand-size discard, [514.1]) are handled first when a step/phase begins, before state-based actions are checked or priority is given ([703.3], [117.3a]).

The one exception to 'only checked when priority would be given' is the cleanup step, where normally no player receives priority at all ([514.3a], [117.3a]). Even there, the game still checks for state-based actions (and waiting triggered abilities) at that point; if any exist, they're performed/put on the stack and the active player then does get priority, per [704.3] and [514.3a]. If none exist, no one gets priority and the step simply ends.

A related but distinct case: some effects that end the combat phase (e.g., an ability like Mandate of Peace's) explicitly call for a state-based action check as part of resolving that effect, per [724.2c], without any player getting priority or triggered abilities going on the stack at that point — this is a special resolution procedure, not the normal priority-driven check.

Finally, state-based actions are not controlled by any player ([704.2]), don't use the stack ([704.1], [704.1a], [405.6f]), and pay no attention to the intermediate game states that occur only *during* the resolution of a spell or ability ([704.4]) — they're checked only at the points described above (before priority, and in the cleanup step / combat-ending exception), not continuously mid-resolution.

This answer applies regardless of player count — none of the cited rules differentiate between two-player and multiplayer games for when state-based actions are checked.

question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer:
The active player is simply the player whose turn it is right now — rule [102.1] defines it that way explicitly ("The active player is the player whose turn it is. The other players are nonactive players."). In a two-player game there's only one other player, who is the nonactive player; in a multiplayer game every player besides the one whose turn it is is a nonactive player [102.1]. Turns rotate around the table, so the active player changes as the game progresses into each new turn.

A few related points worth knowing: the active player gets priority at several key points during a turn — for example at the start of upkeep and draw steps [508.2], [504.2], the start of the main phases [507.2], [505.6], and at the start of the combat damage step [510.3] — because rule [117.1] says whoever has priority may cast spells or activate abilities. During the combat phase, the active player is also the attacking player, and in a two-player game the nonactive player is automatically the defending player [506.2]; in some multiplayer formats the active player instead has to choose which opponent becomes the defending player [507.1].

If multiple players (or, in games using the shared team turns option, multiple teams) need to make simultaneous choices, the active player decides first, then the other players follow in turn order — this is called Active Player, Nonactive Player (APNAP) order [101.4], [101.4e]. If teams take turns together, the whole team whose turn it is is called the "active team," and each other team is a "nonactive team" [805.4a], and APNAP order is modified so the active team's players choose first, in any order they like, before nonactive teams do the same [805.6].

A couple of edge cases: if an ability refers to "the active player" while multiple active players exist (e.g., in shared-team-turn games), its controller chooses which one it means [805.9]. And if a player is being magically controlled by another player during their own turn, they're still considered the active player — only control of the player's actions changes, not who is active [723.3].

question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
answer:
Yes. Whenever you have priority and cast a spell, you get priority back immediately afterward, so you can keep casting additional spells (or activating abilities) before anyone else gets a chance to act — this is commonly called "holding priority."

Here's why: rule [601.2a] and [601.2f] describe the steps for casting a spell (moving it to the stack, determining and paying costs, etc.). Once those steps are finished, rule [601.2i] (and the identical clause restated in [117.3c]) says: "If the spell's controller had priority before casting it, they get priority." So as long as you had priority when you started casting your first spell, you receive priority again the instant it finishes being cast, before it resolves.

Because you now have priority again, rule [117.1] lets you cast another spell (or activate an ability) right then — and rule [117.7] confirms that a spell cast while another spell is already on the stack is cast "in response to" the earlier one, and will resolve first. You can keep doing this, stacking spell on top of spell, for as long as you keep having priority after each cast.

The phase or step won't end while you're doing this: per [500.2], a phase/step only ends when the stack is empty AND all players pass priority in succession — simply emptying the stack isn't enough, and you haven't passed at all while you're holding priority to cast more spells.

Note on player count: rules [117.1], [117.3c], and [601.2a/i] don't distinguish between two-player and multiplayer games — the "you get priority back after casting" rule works the same regardless of how many players are at the table. The one place the number of players matters is in team or Grand Melee variants: in a team game, [805.5a] says priority belongs to the team, not the individual player, so any teammate could act once your team has priority; and in Grand Melee, [807.5b] involves multiple simultaneous stacks, and you'd have to specify which stack each new spell goes on. Outside of those special formats, your ability to hold priority and chain spells works identically whether it's a two-player duel or a larger multiplayer free-for-all.

question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
answer:
Lore counters are added to a Saga at two distinct moments. First, when a Saga enters the battlefield, it enters with a lore counter already on it (or, if it has read ahead, with the chosen number of lore counters) — this is a replacement effect built into the permanent's own "enters with..." ability, not something that happens later [714.3a][714.3b][614.1c]. Second, on every turn after that (including the turn it enters, for Sagas without read ahead), a turn-based action places one lore counter on each Saga a player controls with one or more chapter abilities immediately as that player's precombat main phase begins [703.4f][714.3c][505.4]. This is a turn-based action, so it happens automatically and does not use the stack.

A few related points: only the active player's Sagas get a counter this way, and it's specifically tied to the precombat main phase beginning — it happens before the active player would otherwise get priority in that phase, and (in Archenemy games) after the archenemy's scheme action [703.4f]. Putting the counter(s) on can then cause a chapter ability's triggered condition to be checked (chapter symbols represent triggered abilities that fire when the lore-counter count crosses the threshold, per [107.15a] and [714.2b]). If a Saga has read ahead, chapter abilities for numbers it didn't reach on entry can't trigger the turn it entered unless the lore-counter count exactly matches that chapter number [702.155a]. Finally, once a Saga's lore counters equal or exceed its final chapter number (and no chapter ability from it is still on the stack), a state-based action causes its controller to sacrifice it [704.5s][714.4]; this check happens continuously, not at a fixed turn step.

This is a general answer that applies the same whether there are two players or more than two — the trigger is specifically about the active player's own precombat main phase and their own Sagas, not about opponents, so multiplayer doesn't change the mechanic itself.

question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by a spell or ability as it resolves (or by a replacement effect being applied, or by a static ability that lets a player take an action) that doesn't do anything right away, but instead does something later in the game, usually at a specific future time. [Delayed Triggered Ability] [603.7] Even though it's created at one moment, its actual triggering condition happens later, and it will always contain the word "when," "whenever," or "at" somewhere in its text, even though that word usually isn't the very first word of the ability. [603.7a]

Key points about how delayed triggered abilities work:
- They're created during the resolution of a spell or ability, when a replacement effect is applied, or when a static ability lets a player take an action. [603.7a]
- A delayed triggered ability won't trigger until it has actually been created, even if the event it cares about already happened just before it was created — in that case it simply never triggers. [603.7a]
- Normally it only triggers once, the next time its trigger event happens, unless it has a stated duration like "this turn." If the trigger event happens more than once simultaneously with no stated duration, its controller chooses which occurrence causes it to trigger. [603.7b]

question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
answer:
Yes. Instants and sorceries (non-permanent spells) can have abilities, and in fact almost always do — any text on an instant or sorcery spell counts as a "spell ability" unless it's specifically an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that meets the criteria in rule 113.6 [113.3a]. A spell ability is one that's followed as instructions while the instant or sorcery spell is resolving [113.3a], and it exists as part of that spell object while it's on the stack [113.1c],[113.2d].

It's also possible, though less common, for an instant or sorcery to carry an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability instead of (or alongside) its normal spell ability text. Normally, abilities of an instant or sorcery function only while that object is on the stack, since abilities of objects other than permanents usually only function while the object is in the zone the rules say they function in — permanents' abilities function on the battlefield, while instant/sorcery abilities function on the stack — with certain listed exceptions [113.6]. So the general answer is: a non-permanent spell's text generates a spell ability that operates only during that spell's resolution, but the same object could instead (or in addition) carry an activated, triggered, or static ability if it fits the specific exceptions carved out in rule 113.6.

Note also that any ability, regardless of type, is a characteristic that lets an object affect the game and generates effects when it resolves or triggers [113.1a],[113.2d],[609.1].

question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
answer: Yes. Split second (rule 702.61a) is a static ability that, while the spell is on the stack, prevents players from casting other spells or activating abilities that aren't mana abilities. You can still activate mana abilities to pay costs, generate mana for future use, etc., exactly as you normally could (605.3a, 117.1d), even while a split second spell is on the stack.
